Moina is a small freshwater crustacean closely related to Daphnia and also called a water flea; its brood pouch is open, while Daphnia's is closed.
Adult Moina are 700–1,000 µm long; young Moina are under 400 µm, about the size of adult rotifers.
Newly hatched fry of most freshwater fish species can eat young Moina as their first food.
Brine shrimp (Artemia) nauplii of 500 µm die quickly in freshwater, which makes Moina well suited to freshwater fry.
In Singapore, Moina were the sole food for fry of many ornamental species, with 95–99% survival to ¾ inch (20 mm) common.
Moina protein averages about 50% of dry weight; fat is 20–27% of dry weight in adult females and 4–6% in juveniles.
Bo bo are tiny freshwater crustaceans of the order Cladocera, about 0.2–3.0 mm, living in ponds, marshes and still water and eating algae, bacteria and suspended debris.
The page gives bo bo a protein content of 50–70% of dry weight, plus omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.
Bo bo's live movement triggers hunting and can help picky fish eat; its soft shell and small size suit fry.
Bo bo suit fry and small-mouthed ornamental fish such as guppies (Poecilia), bettas (Betta) and neon tetras (Paracheirodon).
BoBo are small crustaceans mainly of the genera Moina or Daphnia, about 0.3–1 mm long, that swim jerkily and gather in clusters.
BoBo protein can reach about 60%, but quality depends on the water and environment they come from.
Daphnia grow up to about 3 mm long and are fed to fish, tadpoles, salamanders, newts and aquatic insects.
Daphnia eat algae and help clear water; green water is not required to culture them.
Healthy Moina are green or brown-red, with full guts and active movement.
Pale Moina with empty guts, or Moina producing resting eggs, signal poor conditions or too little food.
Choose bo bo starter stock that looks light brown or slightly greenish; pale, whitish stock is weak.
A pale bo bo colony is underfed and should get food right away.
Bo bo are ready to harvest when they form reddish-orange or pink clouds in the water.
A Moina culture is ready for harvest at 45–75 Moina per 1-teaspoon (3–5 ml) sample; the water should look slightly cloudy and tea-coloured or green.
An abrupt drop in food makes Moina switch to sexual reproduction and resting eggs (ephippia).
Poor food or temperature changes trigger males and sexual reproduction in bo bo, which is slow and yields little.
Daphnia cultures crash from rapid breeding in small tanks and from waste building up in small volumes of water.
Use a few dozen litres of container (cement tank, glass tank or plastic basin) to culture bo bo.
About 3 days before stocking bo bo, spread a 1–2 cm layer of rotted cow or pig manure on the container bottom.
Stock roughly one glass of bo bo starter per 20 liters of water.
Around 4–5 days after stocking, once bo bo are multiplying, start feeding finely crushed dried cow dung strained through mesh and stirred into the water.
Harvest bo bo after about 7–10 days, when numbers are high, with a fine net or thin cloth, and rinse them in clean water before feeding.
Culture bo bo in a 20 L or larger foam box, basin or small tank with a wide surface and 20–30 cm of dechlorinated water.
To seed a bo bo culture, add dried banana leaves, dried Terminalia catappa (lá bàng) leaves or a few pieces of treated dried cow dung, and wait for the water to turn pale green before adding bo bo.

Clear water in a bo bo culture means the algae is eaten and more food is needed; baker's yeast mixed in water until slightly milky, rice-washing water, powdered milk or soy flour can be used in very small amounts.
Replace about 20–30% of a bo bo culture's water weekly.
Skim bo bo gently with a fine net without stirring the bottom, and harvest a moderate amount daily so the population recovers.

Moina feed per 100 gal (379 L) to start: 0.3–0.5 oz (8.5–14.2 g) yeast, or 6 oz (170 g) dried chicken or hog manure, or 20 oz (567 g) dried cow or horse manure; add 50–100% of the initial amount about 5 days later.
Inoculate with about 100 Moina per gallon (25/L), 24 hours or more after fertilizing; with yeast a few hours of aeration is enough.
Keep Moina culture pH at 7–8; if pH exceeds 9.5, adjust it with vinegar.
Keep Moina culture depth at or below 3 ft (0.9 m), with 16–20 in (0.4–0.5 m) optimal, and shade it with 50–80% light reduction.
Use gentle aeration for Moina; very small bubbles can get trapped under the carapace.
In semi-continuous Moina culture, harvest no more than 20–25% per day; in batch culture, harvest completely after about 5–10 days and restart.
Stir Moina culture bottom sediments daily to prevent anaerobic conditions.
Daphnia do well at around 68°F (20°C) in wide, shallow tanks.
Feed Daphnia active dry yeast blended with water, or spirulina powder, when the culture water is clear.
Harvested Daphnia should be fed right away or kept in a jar for about an hour.
Moina tolerate 5–31°C daily swings, with an optimum of 24–31°C (75–88°F); they survive short periods above 32°C (90°F), and low temperatures reduce production.
Moina are highly sensitive to pesticides, metals such as copper and zinc, detergents and bleach.
If Hydra, back-swimmers, diving beetles or dragonfly larvae appear in a Moina culture, discard the culture and disinfect the tank.
Disinfect Moina culture containers with a 30% muriatic acid solution or by sun-drying.
Aerate municipal water at least two days to remove chlorine, or use a chlorine neutralizer, before culturing Moina.
Chlorine kills Daphnia, so dechlorinate culture water first.
Protect outdoor Moina cultures from rain and screen out predatory insects.
Always keep several Moina cultures in case one dies off.
Keep at least two bo bo containers so you don't lose your whole supply.
Cover bo bo containers with mesh so insects like bọ gạo and mosquito larvae (lăng quăng) cannot get in.
Cover bo bo tanks with mosquito netting to keep out mosquitoes and dragonflies that lay eggs in the water.
Don't add aquatic plants to a bo bo culture, as they make harvesting difficult.
Keep filamentous algae out of bo bo cultures.
Frequent harvesting helps prevent Daphnia culture crashes.
Keep Daphnia cultures indoors to avoid temperature swings, mosquito larvae and invading copepods (Cyclops).
Wild-caught BoBo can carry bacteria; rinse them in clean water several times, and the page suggests soaking them in dilute salt water or a small amount of gentian violet before feeding.
Overly large, dense Moina can harass or damage fry, so feeding rates should be watched.
Feeding too many bo bo leaves uneaten ones to decay and raise ammonia and nitrite; feed only what fish finish in 2–3 minutes.
Strong direct sun can heat a bo bo culture fast and kill the bo bo.
Overfeeding a bo bo culture with yeast, milk or other supplements fouls the water quickly, shown by a bad smell or scum.
Using bo bo only for betta fry at least one week old, when their mouths are large enough.
Feeding dead or smelly BoBo causes disease in fry.
Wild-caught BoBo live only a few hours out of the water without aeration.
Daphnia keepers often underestimate food needs and growth: Daphnia mature in about eight days and each produces about ten young.
Passing Moina through 500 µm mesh fragments them so they are no longer usable as live food.
Live Moina can be kept refrigerated in clean water for several days; enrich them with algae and yeast before feeding.
Freezing or freeze-drying Moina kills them, lowers nutritional value, makes fry less willing to eat them, and nutrients leach fast into water.
Moina routinely reach 19,000 per gallon (5,000/L), while Daphnia magna egg output drops at 95–115 per gallon (25–30/L).
Bo bo females reproduce asexually from about 3–4 days old, producing broods every 1–2 days of roughly 4–22 young.
BoBo (bọ nước) is the common name in Vietnam for these small freshwater crustaceans.
In Vietnam BoBo are cheap and easy to buy locally or culture in plastic tubs, suiting keepers on a budget or raising many fry.
For expensive ornamental fish, the page suggests Artemia for the first 5–7 days, then switching to BoBo.
Bo bo starter stock can be wild-caught or bought from aquarium food sellers.
